sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes: Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV

steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: In the empty workdir run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into it, then write main.py with `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`, `print(df)`. Run `uv run main.py` to see the 40 x 9 table.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Printed DataFrame summary: 40 rows x 9 columns

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip or a uv virtual environment
Why pandas is imported as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional row/column data
pd.read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Reading the printed DataFrame (rows x columns)

hints: Make sure pandas is installed in the environment you run from: `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`).
Put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py so the relative path in read_csv works.
Your file needs three lines: `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`, and `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py`; the output should end with something like `[40 rows x 9 columns]`.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, giving ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
orders.csv saved in another folder (or as orders.csv.txt), causing FileNotFoundError.
Typing `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read_CSV` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Downloading the GitHub HTML page instead of the raw CSV file, which causes a parser error.
Forgetting `print(df)`, so nothing appears when the script runs.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)

steps.title: Load data in a Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb and in the first cell run `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`. In a second cell run `print(df)`.

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load orders.csv

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a plain .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P > New Jupyter Notebook
Python extension needed for notebooks in VS Code
Cells can be run independently; df stays loaded in memory
Running, deleting cells and clearing outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P), choose "New Jupyter Notebook" and save it as notebook.ipynb next to orders.csv.
In the first cell write `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")`, then run it and pick a Python interpreter when asked.
Add a new cell below and write `print(df)`; run only that cell, since df is already loaded from the first one.
If notebooks aren't available, install the "Python" extension from the Extensions pane in VS Code.
common_mistakes: Saving notebook.ipynb in a different folder from orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Choosing a Python kernel/interpreter that doesn't have pandas installed (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas').
Running the print(df) cell before running the first cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Not having the VS Code Python extension installed, so "New Jupyter Notebook" doesn't appear.
Creating a file named notebook.py instead of notebook.ipynb, so there are no cells.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1 (select a Python kernel), then run cell 2 independently
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In separate cells run `df.head()`, `df.tail()`, `df.info()` and `df.describe()`. Then inspect `df.columns` and `df.index` (RangeIndex 0 to 40).

targets.caption: Column names, dtypes and entry count

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entries, columns and dtypes; why strings show as object
describe() generates descriptive statistics
df.columns lists the column names
df.index is a RangeIndex (start 0, stop 40, step 1)

hints: Put each command in its own cell so you can see every output separately.
head(), tail(), info() and describe() are methods, so they need parentheses. columns and index are attributes and do not.
Make sure the cell that loads df has been run first, or df will be undefined.
df.index should show RangeIndex(start=0, stop=<number of rows>, step=1).
common_mistakes: Running these cells before the cell that loads the CSV, which gives NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError: 'Index' object is not callable.
Writing df.head without parentheses, which prints the method object instead of the rows.
Putting several commands in one cell and only seeing the output of the last one.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb select a column with `df["Country"]` and several with `df[["Country", "Product"]]`. Select rows with `df.iloc[0]` and `df.iloc[10]`, then read `df.iloc[10]["Country"]`.

targets.caption: Selecting two columns returns a DataFrame
Selecting a row by position with iloc

explanations.topic: Indexing a single column returns a pandas Series
A list of column names returns a new DataFrame, not a Series
iloc selects rows by integer position
Pandas types differ from built-in Python types; a row can be indexed by position or column name

hints: Run df.columns first to see the exact column names you can select.
Use one pair of brackets for one column (df["Country"]) and double brackets with a list for several (df[["Country", "Product"]]).
Rows by position use df.iloc[n]. Then index the resulting row by column name, e.g. df.iloc[10]["Country"].
common_mistakes: Using single brackets with two names, df["Country", "Product"], which raises a KeyError instead of using a list.
Misspelling or miscasing a column name ("country" vs "Country") and getting a KeyError.
Writing df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of square brackets.
Using an iloc position past the last row, e.g. 40 in a 40-row frame, which gives IndexError.
steps.code:
df.columns
df["Country"]
len(df["Country"])
set(df["Country"])
df[["Country", "Product"]]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]["Country"]

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter with `df[df["Category"] == "Electronics"]`, combine conditions using `&` and `|` inside parentheses (e.g. with `df["Country"] == "USA"`). Also filter numerically, e.g. `df[df["Quantity"] > 2]`.

targets.caption: Filter rows where Category equals Electronics

explanations.topic: Boolean indexing: df[condition] keeps rows where the condition is True
Empty result means the wrong column was used (Product vs Category)
Combine filters with a single & inside parentheses, not Python's 'and'
Use a single pipe | for OR
Numeric comparisons: >, <, <=, !=

hints: Write a condition on a column, e.g. df["Category"] == "Electronics", then put it inside df[ ... ].
To combine conditions, wrap each one in parentheses and join them with & (and) or | (or).
Example: df[(df["Category"] == "Electronics") & (df["Country"] == "USA")]
For numbers, try df[df["Quantity"] > 2].
common_mistakes: Filtering on the wrong column (e.g. Product instead of Category), which returns an empty table.
Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & / |, which raises a ValueError about the truth value of a Series being ambiguous.
Leaving out the parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |, which causes operator-precedence errors.
Writing = instead of == in the comparison.
Mismatching the case or spelling of a value ("electronics" vs "Electronics").

steps.title: Use string and isin filters
steps.instructions: Filter names with `df[df["CustomerName"].str.startswith("A")]` and `.str.endswith("a")`. Use `df[df["Country"].isin(["USA", "Sweden", "Brazil"])]` and negate it with `~`.

explanations.topic: endswith is case-sensitive (uppercase A returns nothing)
Using .str accessor for string methods like startswith/endswith
isin replaces long combined OR conditions
~ operator reverses a boolean condition

hints: String methods on a column live under the .str accessor: df["CustomerName"].str....
Wrap the condition in df[...] to keep only matching rows, e.g. df[df["CustomerName"].str.startswith("A")].
isin takes a list: df[df["Country"].isin(["USA", "Sweden", "Brazil"])].
Put ~ directly before the condition to invert it: df[~df["Country"].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Calling .startswith directly on the Series without .str (AttributeError).
Using an uppercase 'A' with endswith and getting an empty result: the match is case-sensitive.
Passing values to isin as separate arguments instead of a single list.
Using 'not' or '!' instead of ~ to negate a pandas condition.
Misspelling column names (e.g. 'Customer Name' vs 'CustomerName'), which raises a KeyError.

steps.title: Update data with loc
steps.instructions: Change a value with `df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna ...", "Product"] = "Tim"` and replace countries with `df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"`. Uppercase a whole column with `df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper()`.

targets.caption: Locate rows by condition, then pick the column

explanations.topic: loc locates by label/condition vs iloc by index position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame since multiple rows can match
Adding a column after the comma and assigning updates the matching rows
Conditional replacement updates all matching rows at once
Reassigning a column with .str.upper() transforms every value

hints: Use df.loc[condition, column] = new_value: the rows go before the comma and the column goes after it.
The condition is a boolean Series, like df["Country"] == "USA". Put it inside df.loc[...].
Check the exact column name first (e.g. "Product", not "ProductName"). Print df.columns if unsure.
For the whole column, write df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper(). Then display df["Country"] to confirm.
common_mistakes: Using df.iloc with a condition instead of df.loc.
Writing df[df["Country"]=="USA"]["Country"] = ... (chained indexing). This raises SettingWithCopyWarning and doesn't update df.
Misspelling the column name, so pandas creates a new column or raises a KeyError.
Calling .upper() directly on the Series instead of .str.upper().
Forgetting to assign the result back: df["Country"].str.upper() alone doesn't change df.
Re-checking for "United States" after uppercasing, which finds no rows.
steps.code:
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna ..."]
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna ...", "Product"] = "Tim"
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna ..."]

df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"
df[df["Country"] == "USA"]
df[df["Country"] == "United States"]

df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper()
df["Country"]

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with `df = df.drop(39)` and check with `df.tail()`, then reload the CSV. Run `df.dropna()`, `df.fillna(...)` with `inplace=True`, and `df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)`.

targets.caption: Renamed column appears in the header

explanations.topic: df.drop removes the row at a given index label
dropna removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing them
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with df.rename(columns=...)

hints: Every step here is a method on your DataFrame: drop, dropna, fillna, rename.
drop() returns a new DataFrame, so assign it back: df = df.drop(39). Then run df.tail() to check.
For fillna and rename, pass inplace=True so df itself changes.
rename takes a dict: df.rename(columns={"OldName": "New Name"}, inplace=True). Then print df to see the new header.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning back to df, so the row still appears.
Running the drop cell twice and getting a KeyError because index 39 is already gone. Reload the CSV first.
Passing a plain dict to rename without columns=, which renames index labels instead of columns.
Expecting df.dropna() to change df when inplace=True isn't set and the result isn't assigned.
Misspelling the existing column name in rename. Pandas silently ignores it and nothing changes.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# (reload the CSV, e.g. df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"))

df.dropna()

df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save
steps.instructions: Run `df["Country"].value_counts()`, `df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum()` and `df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False)`. Save the result with `df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)`.

explanations.topic: value_counts counts occurrences of each value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY, then aggregates with sum
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv saves the DataFrame; index=False omits the index column

hints: Each of these is a single line in its own cell, called on your DataFrame df.
value_counts is called on one column: df["Country"].value_counts().
For grouping: df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum(); for sorting: df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False).
Save with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False) and check the file browser for new_file.csv.
common_mistakes: Typing df.to_csv as df.2csv (it is to_csv, said aloud as 'to CSV').
Calling value_counts on the whole DataFrame instead of the Country column.
Forgetting the column selection ["Price"] before .sum(), which sums every numeric column.
Leaving ascending=True (or omitting it) when you want the highest prices first.
Price column stored as strings, so sum concatenates or sort_values sorts alphabetically. Clean or convert it first.
Column name case mismatch (e.g. "country" vs "Country") causing a KeyError.
steps.code:
df["Country"].value_counts()

df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum()

df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False)

df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)
